en: Dīgha Nikāya 1:
Brahmajāla Sutta 1.
Discussion with Wanderers
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was traveling along the highway between Rājagaha and Nāḷandā together with a large Saṅgha of monks, numbering about five hundred.
And the wanderer Suppiya was also traveling along the highway between Rājagaha and Nāḷandā together with his pupil, the young Brahmin Brahmadatta.
Thereupon, the wanderer Suppiya spoke in many ways in dispraise of the Buddha, in dispraise of the Dhamma, and in dispraise of the Saṅgha;
but the young Brahmin Brahmadatta, a pupil of the wanderer Suppiya, spoke in many ways in praise of the Buddha, in praise of the Dhamma, and in praise of the Saṅgha.
Thus both the teacher and the pupil followed closely behind the Blessed One and the community of monks, each maintaining a doctrine that was the direct opposite of the other.
Then the Blessed One took up residence for one night at the royal pavilion in Ambalaṭṭhikā together with the community of monks.
The wanderer Suppiya also took up residence for one night at the royal pavilion in Ambalaṭṭhikā with his pupil, the young Brahmin Brahmadatta.
There, indeed, the wanderer Suppiya spoke in many ways in dispraise of the Buddha, in dispraise of the Dhamma, and in dispraise of the Saṅgha;
yet the young Brahmin Brahmadatta, who was the pupil of the wanderer Suppiya, spoke in many ways in praise of the Buddha, in praise of the Dhamma, and in praise of the Saṅgha.
Thus those two, teacher and pupil, lived as direct opposites in their speech toward one another.
Then, as many bhikkhus who had risen at the time of dawn were sitting together and assembled in the pavilion, this reasoned reflection arose among them:

“It is wonderful, friends! It is marvelous, friends! To what an extent the diversity of beings’ inclinations has been thoroughly understood by the Blessed One, the knower, the seer, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One!”
For this wanderer Suppiya speaks in many ways in dispraise of the Buddha, in dispraise of the Dhamma, and in dispraise of the Saṅgha;
yet the young Brahmin Brahmadatta, a pupil of the wanderer Suppiya, speaks in many ways in praise of the Buddha, in praise of the Dhamma, and in praise of the Saṅgha.
“Thus both the teacher and the pupil followed closely behind the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, each propounding a view that was the direct opposite of the other.

Then the Blessed One, having understood this summary of the matter among those bhikkhus, went to the pavilion; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, for what discussion are you gathered and seated here now? And what was the conversation of yours that remained unfinished?”
When this was said, those bhikkhus said to the Blessed One:
"Here, Bhante, as we had risen at the time of dawn and were sitting gathered together in the assembly hall, this reflection arose among us:

'It is wonderful, friends! It is marvelous, friends! To what an extent the diversity of beings' inclinations has been thoroughly understood by that Blessed One, the Knower, the Seer, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One!'"
For this wanderer Suppiya speaks in many ways in dispraise of the Buddha, in dispraise of the Dhamma, and in dispraise of the Saṅgha;
yet the young Brahmin Brahmadatta, a pupil of the wanderer Suppiya, speaks in many ways in praise of the Buddha, in praise of the Dhamma, and in praise of the Saṅgha.
“Thus, both the teacher and the pupil followed closely behind the Blessed One and the community of monks, each speaking in direct opposition to the other.
‘Venerable sir, this was our conversation that remained unfinished when the Blessed One arrived.
‘Monks, if others should speak dispraise of me, or speak dispraise of the Dhamma, or speak dispraise of the Saṅgha, you should not harbor resentment, ill will, or mental displeasure toward them.’”
Monks, if others should speak in dispraise of me, or speak in dispraise of the Dhamma, or speak in dispraise of the Saṅgha,
and if you were thereby angry or displeased, that would indeed be an obstacle for you. Monks,
if others should speak in dispraise of me, or speak in dispraise of the Dhamma, or speak in dispraise of the Saṅgha...
“Or if they were to speak dispraise of you, and if you were thereupon angry or displeased,
would you still be able to discern what was well-spoken and what was ill-spoken by others?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”

“Monks, if others should speak dispraise of me, or speak dispraise of the Dhamma, or speak dispraise of the Saṅgha, you should there disentangle what is untrue from its untruth, saying: ‘In this way it is untrue;
in this way it is incorrect; this does not exist among us, nor is this found among us.’”
“Monks, if others should speak in praise of me, or speak in praise of the Dhamma, or speak in praise of the Saṅgha, you should not feel delight, joy, or elation of heart on that account. Monks,
if others should speak in praise of me, or speak in praise of the Dhamma, or speak in praise of the Saṅgha, and if you were to feel delighted,
joyful, and elated on that account, it would be an obstacle for you.”
“Monks, if others should speak in praise of me, or speak in praise of the Dhamma, or speak in praise of the Saṅgha, you should acknowledge what is true as true: ‘Thus it is true;
thus it is factual; this exists among us, and this is indeed found among us. 2.
Virtue (Sīla)
2.1. Minor Virtue.
“But this, bhikkhus, is a minor, petty, mere matter of virtue by which an ordinary person might speak in praise of the Tathāgata.
And what, bhikkhus, is that minor, petty, mere matter of virtue by which an ordinary person might speak in praise of the Tathāgata?”

‘Having abandoned the taking of life, the ascetic Gotama abstains from taking life; he has laid aside the rod and the sword, and dwells conscientious, compassionate, and sympathetic toward the welfare of all living beings’—thus, monks, an ordinary person might speak when praising the Tathāgata.

‘Having abandoned taking what is not given, the ascetic Gotama abstains from taking what is not given; he takes only what is given, expects only what is given, and dwells with himself pure and free from theft.’
For it is thus, monks, that an ordinary person might speak in praise of the Tathāgata:
‘Having abandoned unchastity, the ascetic Gotama lives a life of celibacy; he is one who dwells apart, abstaining from sexual intercourse, the common practice of the village.
It is thus, monks, that an ordinary person might speak in praise of the Tathāgata.
‘Having abandoned false speech, the ascetic Gotama abstains from false speech;
he is a speaker of truth, one devoted to truth, trustworthy, reliable, and not a deceiver of the world’—thus, monks, an ordinary person might speak when speaking in praise of the Tathāgata.
‘Having abandoned malicious speech, the ascetic Gotama abstains from malicious speech; having heard something here, he does not [repeat it] there...’
‘He does not report what he has heard here for the sake of dividing those people there, nor does he report what he has heard there for the sake of dividing these people here.

Thus, he is a reconciler of those who are divided, or a promoter of the harmony of those who are united; he delights in concord, rejoices in concord, finds joy in concord, and speaks words that bring about concord.
In this way, monks, an ordinary person might speak in praise of the Tathāgata.

‘Having abandoned harsh speech, the ascetic Gotama abstains from harsh speech; he speaks such words as are gentle, pleasing to the ear, endearing, heart-reaching, urbane, agreeable to many people, and dear to many people’—thus, monks, an ordinary person might speak when praising the Tathāgata.
‘Having abandoned idle chatter, the ascetic Gotama abstains from idle chatter; he speaks at the proper time, speaks what is true...’
‘He speaks what is beneficial, he speaks what is Dhamma, he speaks what is Vinaya;
he utters speech that is timely, founded on fact, relevant, connected with the goal, and purposeful’—thus indeed, monks, would an ordinary person speak when praising the Tathāgata.
‘The ascetic Gotama abstains from the destruction of seeds and plants.’”
For it is said thus, monks:
“… The ascetic Gotama eats but one meal a day; he refrains from eating at night and abstains from food outside the proper time.
The ascetic Gotama abstains from watching dancing, singing, music, and performances of a frivolous nature.”
The ascetic Gotama abstains from wearing garlands, using scents and unguents,
and from adorning and beautifying himself with ornaments… The ascetic Gotama abstains from high and luxurious beds and seats… The ascetic Gotama abstains from accepting gold and silver…
The ascetic Gotama abstains from accepting raw grain...
The ascetic Gotama abstains from accepting raw meat...
The ascetic Gotama abstains from accepting women and girls...
The ascetic Gotama abstains from accepting female and male slaves...
The ascetic Gotama abstains from accepting goats and sheep...
The ascetic Gotama abstains from accepting chickens and pigs...
The ascetic Gotama abstains from accepting elephants, cattle, horses, and mares...
The ascetic Gotama abstains from accepting fields and land...
The ascetic Gotama abstains from engaging in the business of acting as a messenger or an envoy...
The ascetic Gotama abstains from buying and selling...
The ascetic Gotama abstains from false weights, false metals, and false measures...
The ascetic Gotama abstains from bribery, cheating, fraud, and crooked ways.
‘The ascetic Gotama abstains from cutting, killing, binding, robbing, plundering,
and using force’— thus, monks, would an ordinary person speak when praising the Tathāgata.
The Shorter Code of Ethics is finished.
2.2. The Middle Section on Virtue:
“Furthermore, there are certain venerable recluses and brahmins who, having eaten food given in faith, remain devoted to such destruction of seeds and living beings as these:
namely, plants propagated from roots, from stems, from joints, from cuttings, and fifthly, those propagated from seeds.”
‘The ascetic Gotama abstains from such undertakings as the destruction of seeds and the destruction of living plants’—
thus, monks, an ordinary person might speak when praising the Tathāgata.
Or again, monks, some worthy recluses and brahmins, having eaten meals given in faith, continue to live devoted to such enjoyment of stored-up goods.
‘For example—the storage of food, the storage of drink, the storage of clothing, the storage of vehicles, the storage of bedding, the storage of perfumes, and the storage of meat;
the ascetic Gotama abstains from such enjoyment of stored-up goods.
Thus, monks, an ordinary person might speak when speaking in praise of the Tathāgata.
‘Or again, there are certain venerable recluses and brahmins who, having eaten food given in faith, remain devoted to such frivolous spectacles as these:
namely, dancing, singing, instrumental music, theatrical performances, storytelling, hand-clapping, drumming, cymbals, tambourines, acrobatics,
mimes, clowns, reed-pipes, water-splashing, elephant fights, horse fights, buffalo fights, bull fights, [and so forth].’

‘The ascetic Gotama abstains from such spectacles as bullfights, ramfights, cockfights, quailfights, stick-fighting, boxing, wrestling, sham-fights, military parades, the array of troops, and the review of troops.’”
For it is thus, monks, that an ordinary person might speak in praise of the Tathāgata:
"Or rather, there are certain venerable recluses and brahmins who, having eaten food given in faith, remain devoted to such grounds for negligence as gambling, namely:
the eight-row game, the ten-row game, *ākāsa*, *parihārapatha*, *santika*, *khalika*, and *ghaṭika*."

‘The ascetic Gotama abstains from such gambling and places of negligence as dice with men, stick-games, hand-sticks, “crab” games, “the snare,” tossing up, tip-cat, board-games, toy-carts, bow-and-arrow play, chariot-racing, archery, letter-guessing, and mind-reading, as well as similar practices.’”
For it is thus, monks, that an ordinary person might speak in praise of the Tathāgata:
"Or rather, there are certain venerable recluses and brahmins who, having eaten meals given out of faith, remain devoted to such high and luxurious beds and seats as these:
namely, a divan, a couch, a woolen rug, a variegated coverlet, a white woolen rug, a long-haired rug, a cotton-down quilt, and a silk rug."

‘The ascetic Gotama abstains from high and luxurious beds and seats, such as those with hair on both sides, hair on one side, woven silk, embroidered cloth, elephant-horse-carpet covers, chariot-covers, antelope skins, or the choice hide of the kadali-deer, including those with canopies and red pillows at both ends.’”
For it is thus, monks, that an ordinary person might speak in praise of the Tathāgata.
Or else, just as some venerable recluses and brahmins, having eaten meals provided out of faith, remain devoted to such practices of adornment and decoration as these:
rubbing [the body] with unguents, massaging, bathing, anointing, looking in mirrors, applying collyrium, wearing garlands, scents, and ointments, and using face-powder.
‘The ascetic Gotama abstains from such practices as smearing the face, binding the hands, binding the topknot, carrying a staff, a tube, a sword, a parasol, variegated sandals,
a turban, a jewel, a yak-tail fan, and white garments with long fringes;
he abstains from such engagements in adorning and beautifying oneself.’”
For it is thus, monks, that an ordinary person might speak in praise of the Tathāgata:
"Or rather, there are certain venerable recluses and brahmins who, having eaten food given in faith, dwell devoted to such frivolous talk as this:
talk of kings, talk of thieves, talk of ministers, talk of armies, talk of dangers, talk of battles..."
Talk about food, talk about drinks, talk about clothing, talk about bedding, talk about garlands, talk about scents, talk about relatives, talk about vehicles, talk about villages,
talk about market towns, talk about cities, talk about countries, talk about women, talk about heroes,

talk about streets, talk about wells, talk about the departed ancestors, various kinds of nonsensical chatter, talk about worldly speculation, talk about the ocean, and talk about "thus it was" and "thus it will be."
‘The ascetic Gotama abstains from such frivolous talk as this’—thus, monks, an ordinary person might speak when praising the Tathāgata. Or again:
‘While some worthy ascetics and brahmins, having eaten meals provided out of faith, remain devoted to such contentious talk as this…’
That is to say: "You do not understand this Dhamma and Discipline;
I understand this Dhamma and Discipline. How could you understand this Dhamma and Discipline? You have practiced wrongly; I have practiced rightly.
My [position] is consistent; yours is inconsistent. What should have been said first, you said last; what should have been said last, you said first."

‘The ascetic Gotama abstains from such contentious talk as: “What you have practiced has been overturned; your thesis has been refuted; you are defeated; go, seek release from your position, or find another way out if you can!”’—thus he speaks.
For it is thus, monks, that an ordinary person might speak in praise of the Tathāgata:

"Or rather, there are certain venerable recluses and brahmins who, having eaten meals given out of faith, remain devoted to the practice of running errands and acting as messengers, such as for kings, royal ministers, kshatriyas, brahmins, householders, or princes, [saying]: 'Go here, go there; take this, bring that from there.'"
‘The ascetic Gotama abstains from such errands as these, involving going and returning as a messenger’—thus, monks, an ordinary person might speak when praising the Tathāgata.
Or again: ‘Just as some worthy recluses and brahmins, having eaten meals given in faith, are deceivers, talkers, seekers of hints, flatterers, and those who strive to win gain with gain.’
‘The ascetic Gotama abstains from such forms of hypocrisy and flattery’—
thus, monks, an ordinary person might speak when praising the Tathāgata.
The Middle Section on Virtue is finished.
2.3. The Great Virtue:
“Or again, certain venerable recluses and brahmins, having eaten food given in faith, make their living by such low arts and wrong livelihoods as these:
namely, the science of limbs, omens, portents, dreams, bodily marks, mouse-bites, fire-sacrifices, and grass-sacrifices.”

Thus: the burnt-offering of husks, the burnt-offering of chaff, the burnt-offering of rice grains, the burnt-offering of ghee, the burnt-offering of oil, the mouth-burnt-offering, the blood-burnt-offering;

the science of limbs, the science of sites, the science of chariots, the science of prosperity, the science of spirits, the science of abundance, the science of snakes, the science of poisons, the science of scorpions, the science of rats, the science of birds, the science of crows, the meditation on cooked food, the protection against arrows, and the deer-cycle.
‘The ascetic Gotama abstains from such base arts and wrong livelihood as this’—
thus, monks, an ordinary person might speak when speaking in praise of the Tathāgata.
Or again, ‘While some worthy recluses and brahmins, having consumed food given in faith, maintain their lives by such base arts and wrong livelihood as this…’

Namely: the characteristics of gems, the characteristics of garments, the characteristics of staffs, the characteristics of swords, the characteristics of blades, the characteristics of spears, the characteristics of bows,
the characteristics of weapons, the characteristics of women, the characteristics of men, the characteristics of boys,

the characteristics of girls, the characteristics of male slaves, the characteristics of female slaves, the characteristics of elephants, the characteristics of horses, and the characteristics of oxen.
‘The ascetic Gotama abstains from such wrong livelihood as the science of omens concerning bulls, cows, goats, rams, chickens, quails, iguanas, lizards, tortoises, and deer.
Thus he refrains from such low arts.
For it is thus, bhikkhus, that an ordinary person might speak when praising the Tathāgata:
"Or else, there are certain venerable recluses and brahmins who, having eaten meals given out of faith, maintain their lives by such low arts and wrong livelihoods as these:
'There will be a military expedition for the kings; there will be no military expedition for the kings'; [or regarding] those within the kingdom..."
There will be the arrival of kings; there will be the departure of foreign kings;
there will be the arrival of foreign kings; there will be the departure of internal kings;
there will be victory for the internal kings; there will be defeat for the foreign kings; there will be victory for the foreign kings.

‘There will be defeat for internal kings; thus there will be victory for this one, and thus there will be defeat for that one’—in such a way, monks, an ordinary person might speak when speaking in praise of the Tathāgata, saying: ‘The ascetic Gotama abstains from such base arts as these, which constitute a wrong livelihood.’”
‘Or how some venerable recluses and brahmins, having eaten food given in faith, make their living by such base arts and wrong livelihood as this:
“There will be an eclipse of the moon; there will be an eclipse of the sun; there will be an eclipse of a constellation;
there will be the deviation of the moon and sun from their paths; there will be the deviation of the moon and sun from their courses.”’
There will be the favorable course of the constellations; there will be the unfavorable course of the constellations;
there will be a falling of meteors; there will be a blazing of the quarters; there will be an earthquake; there will be thunder from the gods;
there will be the rising, setting, defilement, and purification of the moon, sun, and constellations; and there will be an eclipse of the moon with such-and-such a result.
"Such will be the ripening of an eclipse of the sun; such will be the ripening of an eclipse of a constellation;
such will be the ripening of the moon and sun going on their proper course; such will be the ripening of the moon and sun going off their proper course;
such will be the ripening of the constellations going on their proper course; such will be the ripening of the constellations..."
There will be wandering onto wrong paths; such will be the ripening of the falling of meteors; such will be the ripening of the blazing of the quarters;
such will be the ripening of the earthquake; such will be the ripening of the thundering of the gods;
such will be the ripening of the rising, setting, defilement, and purification of the moon, the sun, and the constellations.
‘The ascetic Gotama abstains from such base arts and wrong livelihood as this’—thus, monks, would an ordinary person speak when speaking in praise of the Tathāgata. Or again:
‘While some worthy ascetics and brahmins, having eaten food given out of faith, make their living by such base arts and wrong livelihood as this.’
Namely: there will be good rain; there will be bad rain; there will be abundance of food;
there will be scarcity of food; there will be safety; there will be danger; there will be disease; there will be health;
[and] finger-calculation, arithmetic, accounting, poetry, and cosmology.
‘The ascetic Gotama abstains from such base arts and wrong livelihood as these’—thus, monks, would an ordinary person speak when praising the Tathāgata. Or again:
‘While some worthy recluses and brahmins, having consumed food given in faith, make their living by such base arts and wrong livelihoods, [the ascetic Gotama does not].’”
Namely: bringing together, marrying off, concealing, revealing, gathering, scattering, making fortunate, making unfortunate, causing miscarriage,
binding the tongue, joining the jaw, beckoning with the hand, beckoning with the jaw,
beckoning with the ear, the mirror-question, the maiden-question, the deity-question, and the worship of the sun.
‘The ascetic Gotama abstains from such wrong livelihood as the practice of divination by the great stars, fire-sacrifices, and invoking the goddess Siri’—
it is in this way, monks, that an ordinary person might speak when praising the Tathāgata.
‘Or again, certain venerable recluses and brahmins, having eaten food given in faith, make their living by such low arts and wrong livelihood as these:
rites for the propitiation of deities, rites of consecration, rites for the spirits, rites for the spirits of the earth, rites for rain, rites for prosperity,
rites for land, rites for the preparation of land, ritual rinsing, ritual bathing, burnt offerings, emetics, purgatives, and catheters.’

‘The ascetic Gotama abstains from such wrong livelihood as the practice of downward purgatives, head-purgatives, ear-oils, eye-salves, nasal medicines, collyriums, counter-collyriums, surgery, midwifery, and the administration of medicinal roots and the extraction of herbal decoctions.’— thus he speaks.
For it is thus, monks, that an ordinary person might speak when praising the Tathāgata.
This, monks, is merely trifling, merely insignificant, merely a matter of virtue, by which an ordinary person might speak when praising the Tathāgata.
The Great Virtue (Mahāsīla) is concluded.

3. Views 3.1. Speculators Concerning the Past There are, monks, other phenomena that are deep, difficult to see, difficult to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of mere reasoning, [and so forth].
These things, monks, are subtle, to be realized by the wise, which the Tathāgata, having realized them for himself through direct knowledge, proclaims;
and it is concerning these that those speaking rightly would describe the Tathāgata as he truly is.
And what, monks, are those things that are deep, hard to see, hard to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of mere reasoning?
Subtle and to be realized by the wise—those things which the Tathāgata, having realized them for himself through direct knowledge, proclaims;
those things by which one speaking rightly would describe the Tathāgata as he truly is.

There are, monks, some recluses and brahmins who are speculators about the past, who hold views regarding the past, and who assert various doctrinal propositions concerning the past based on eighteen grounds.

And on what basis, with reference to what, do those venerable recluses and brahmins, being speculators about the past and holding views regarding the past, assert various doctrinal positions concerning the past based on eighteen grounds?
3.1.1. Eternalism:
There are, monks, some recluses and brahmins who are eternalists; they proclaim the self and the world to be eternal on four grounds.
And on what basis, on what account do those worthy recluses and brahmins, being eternalists, proclaim the self and the world to be eternal through four grounds?
Here, monks, a certain recluse or brahmin, by means of ardor, exertion, application, heedfulness, and right attention,
attains such a concentration of mind that, when his mind is thus concentrated...
With his mind, he recollects his manifold past abodes,
that is to say: one birth, two births, three births, four births,
five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births...
One hundred births, one thousand births, one hundred thousand births; many hundreds of births, many thousands of births, many hundreds of thousands of births:
"In that place I was, with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan;
passing away from there, I arose in another place; there too I was, with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance..."
‘Such was my food, such was my experience of pleasure and pain, such was the limit of my lifespan; passing away from there, I reappeared here.
Thus he recollects his manifold past lives in their modes and details.
He says this:
‘The self and the world are eternal, barren, fixed as a mountain peak, standing firm like a pillar;
these beings run on and wander about, pass away and reappear, yet they remain exactly the same for all eternity.
For what reason? Because...’
For by means of ardor, exertion, application, heedfulness, and right attention, I attain such a concentration of mind that, with my mind thus concentrated, I recollect various past lives.
That is to say: one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, and fifty births.
One hundred births, one thousand births, one hundred thousand births, many hundreds of births, many thousands of births, many hundreds of thousands of births:
"In that place I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a lifespan;
passing away from there, I arose in another place; there too I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance..."
“Such was my food, such was my experience of pleasure and pain, such was the limit of my lifespan; passing away from there, I reappeared here.
Thus I recollect my manifold past lives in their modes and details.
By this means I know this:
‘The self and the world are eternal, barren, fixed as a mountain peak, standing firm like a pillar;
these beings run on and wander about, pass away and reappear, yet they remain exactly the same for all eternity.
This, monks, is the first position, based upon which and referring to which some ascetics and brahmins, being eternalists, proclaim the self and the world to be eternal.
And on what basis, on what account, do those venerable recluses and brahmins, being eternalists, proclaim the self and the world to be eternal?
Here, monks, a certain recluse or brahmin, through ardor, through exertion, through application, through diligence, and through right attention,
attains such a concentration of mind that, when his mind is thus concentrated...
With his mind, he recollects his manifold past abodes.

That is to say: one eon of dissolution and evolution, two eons of dissolution and evolution, three eons of dissolution and evolution, four eons of dissolution and evolution, five eons of dissolution and evolution, ten eons of dissolution and evolution: "In that place, I was..."
‘I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan;
passing away from there, I arose elsewhere; there too I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan;
passing away from there, I was reborn here. Thus, with its modes and particulars, he recollects his manifold past lives.
He recollects his past lives.
He speaks thus:
“The self and the world are eternal, barren, fixed, and established like a pillar.”
And those beings run on and wander about, passing away and being reborn; yet indeed, there is something that remains eternal.
For what reason?

Because, through ardor, through striving, through application, through diligence, and through right attention, I have attained such a concentration of mind that, with my mind thus concentrated, I recollect my manifold past lives.
That is to say— one eon of dissolution and evolution, two eons of dissolution and evolution, three eons of dissolution and evolution,
four eons of dissolution and evolution, five eons of dissolution and evolution, or ten eons of dissolution and evolution: "In that place I was, with such a name, such a clan,
such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan."
"Having passed away from there, I arose there; there I was with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan;
having passed away from there, I have reappeared here. Thus I recollect my manifold past lives in their modes and details.
"By this means I know this:

'The self and the world are eternal, barren, steadfast as a mountain peak, standing firm like a pillar; these beings run on and wander about, passing away and being reborn, yet they remain exactly the same for all eternity.
Monks, this is the second ground by resorting to which and depending upon which some recluses and brahmins, proponents of eternalism, declare the self and the world to be eternal.
And on what basis, monks, do those venerable recluses and brahmins, on what grounds, proclaim eternalism, asserting that both the self and the world are eternal?
Here, monks, a certain recluse or brahmin, through ardor, exertion, application, heedfulness, and right attention,
attains such a concentration of mind that, when his mind is thus concentrated...
With his mind, he recollects his manifold past abodes.

That is to say: ten eons of world-dissolution and evolution, twenty eons of world-dissolution and evolution, thirty eons of world-dissolution and evolution, forty eons of world-dissolution and evolution:
"In that place, I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food..."
‘Experiencing such pleasure and pain, having such a lifespan, passing away from there, I arose elsewhere;
there too I was with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, experiencing such pleasure and pain, having such a lifespan, and passing away from there, I reappeared here.
Thus he recollects his manifold past abodes with their modes and details.
Thus he says:
‘The self and the world are eternal, barren, fixed as a mountain peak, standing firm like a pillar;
these beings run on and wander about, pass away and reappear, yet they remain exactly the same for all eternity.’

And why is that? Because, through ardor, exertion, application, diligence, and right attention, I attain such a concentration of mind that, with my mind thus concentrated, I recollect various past lives.
That is to say: ten eons of world-dissolution and evolution, twenty eons of world-dissolution and evolution, and thirty eons of world-dissolution and evolution.

I recall forty eons of world-dissolution and evolution: "In that place I was, with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan; passing away from there, I arose elsewhere;
there too I was, with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan."
“Passing away from there, I was reborn here. Thus I recollect my manifold past lives in their modes and details.
By this means I know:

“The self and the world are eternal, barren, fixed as a mountain peak, standing firm like a pillar; these beings run on and wander about, pass away and are reborn, yet they remain exactly the same for all eternity.”
"This, monks, is the third ground, relying upon which and referring to which some recluses and brahmins proclaim an eternalist view, asserting that the self and the world are eternal.
And as for the fourth, venerable sirs, what do those recluses and brahmins rely upon, what do they refer to, when they proclaim an eternalist view, asserting that the self and the world are eternal?

Here, monks, a certain recluse or brahmin is a reasoner, an investigator; he, having reached a conclusion through reasoning and following the course of investigation, speaks according to his own inspired intuition thus:"
‘The self and the world are eternal, barren, fixed as a mountain peak, standing firm like a pillar;
these beings run on and wander about, pass away and reappear, yet they remain exactly the same for all eternity.
This, monks, is the fourth ground by relying upon which, and referring to which, some ascetics and brahmins who are eternalists proclaim the self and the world to be eternal.
“Monks, it is on these four grounds that those recluses and brahmins who are eternalists proclaim the self and the world to be eternal.
Whatever recluses or brahmins, monks, are eternalists and proclaim the self and the world to be eternal, they all do so on these very four grounds or on one of them;
there is nothing beyond this. And this, monks, the Tathāgata understands.”

‘These standpoints for views, thus grasped and thus adhered to, lead to such-and-such a destination and such-and-such a future state,’ this the Tathāgata understands, and he understands even more than that; yet he does not adhere to that knowledge. Because he does not adhere, the Tathāgata has personally realized Nibbāna.
Having understood, as they really are, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding feelings, the Tathāgata, monks, is liberated through non-clinging.
“Monks, these phenomena are indeed profound, difficult to see, difficult to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of mere reasoning,
subtle, and to be experienced by the wise; they are those which the Tathāgata, having realized them for himself through direct higher knowledge, makes known,
and it is regarding these that those who would speak rightly of the Tathāgata’s true praise would speak.”
The First Recitation Section.
3.1.2. The Doctrine of Partial Eternity.

"Bhikkhus, there are some recluses and brahmins who are partial-eternalists and partial-non-eternalists; on four grounds, they proclaim the self and the world to be partly eternal and partly non-eternal."
And on what basis, with reference to what, do those venerable recluses and brahmins, based on four grounds, proclaim the self and the world to be partly eternal and partly non-eternal?
There comes a time, monks, when after the lapse of a long period this world contracts.
When the world is contracting, beings for the most part are reborn in the Ābhassara (Radiant) Brahmā-world.
There they dwell, mind-made, feeding on rapture, self-luminous, moving through the air, abiding in beauty, remaining for a long, vast duration of time.
There comes a time, monks, when after the passing of a long period, this world expands.
As the world expands, an empty Brahma-palace appears.
Then, a certain being—due to the exhaustion of his lifespan or the exhaustion of his merit—passed away from the Ābhassara realm and was reborn in the empty Brahma palace.
There he dwelt, mind-made, feeding on rapture, self-luminous, moving through the air, established in beauty, and remained for a long, extended period of time.
Because he had lived there alone for so long, a sense of dissatisfaction and agitation arose within him:
‘Oh, if only other beings too might come to this state!
Then, through the exhaustion of their lifespan or the exhaustion of their merit, other beings fall from the Ābhassara realm and are reborn in the Brahma-mansion to be the companions of that being.
There they dwell, mind-made, feeding on rapture, self-luminous, moving through the air, established in beauty, and they remain for a very long time.
In that regard, monks, the being who was first reborn there thinks thus:

"I am Brahmā, the Great Brahmā, the Vanquisher, the Unvanquished, the All-Seeing, the All-Powerful, the Lord, the Maker, the Creator, the Chief, the Appointer, the Father of all beings that have been and are to be.
By me were these beings created."
For what reason?
Because previously this thought occurred to me:
"O, may other beings also come to this state!"
‘Such was my mental aspiration, and these beings have come to this state.
And as for those beings who were reborn later, they too think:

‘This venerable Brahmā is the Great Brahmā, the Conqueror, the Unconquered, the All-Seeing, the All-Powerful, the Lord, the Maker, the Creator, the Chief, the Ordainer, the Father of all that has been and will be.’”
‘We have been created by this Lord Brahmā.
Why is that? Because we saw him first born here, while we were born afterwards.’”
In that regard, monks, the being who was reborn there first is longer-lived, more beautiful, and more influential than those beings who were reborn later.
Those beings who were reborn later are shorter-lived, less beautiful, and less influential.
Moreover, monks, it is possible that some being, having passed away from that body, comes to this state of existence.
Having come to this state, he goes forth from the home life into homelessness.
Having gone forth from the home life into homelessness, through ardor, through exertion,
through application, through diligence, and through right attention, he attains such a concentration of mind that, when his mind is thus concentrated...
In his mind, he recollects that past life, but does not recollect anything beyond it.
He says this:
“That Blessed One Brahmā, the Great Brahmā, the Conqueror, the Unconquered, the All-Seeing, the Sovereign—”
‘The Lord is the creator, the fashioner, the supreme, the architect, the controller, the father of all that has been and shall be.
He by whom we were created, that Blessed Brahmā, is permanent, stable, eternal, unchanging by nature, and he will remain exactly so for all eternity.
But we, who have been created by that Blessed Brahmā, are impermanent, unstable, short-lived, subject to passing away, and have come to this state of existence.’”

This, monks, is the first ground, relying upon which and referring to which, some recluses and brahmins are partial-eternalists and partial-non-eternalists, and they proclaim the self and the world to be partly eternal and partly non-eternal.

And what, friends, is the second ground, relying upon which and referring to which, those venerable recluses and brahmins are partial-eternalists and partial-non-eternalists, and they proclaim the self and the world to be partly eternal and partly non-eternal?
“Bhikkhus, there are gods called ‘Corrupted by Play. They dwell excessively devoted to the practice of laughter, play, and amusement.
As they dwell thus excessively devoted to laughter, play, and amusement, their mindfulness lapses.
With the lapse of mindfulness, those gods fall from that realm.”
"It is indeed possible, monks, that a certain being, having passed away from that body, comes to this state of existence.
Having come to this state of existence, he goes forth from the household life into homelessness.
Having gone forth from the household life into homelessness, through ardor, through exertion, and through application..."
Through diligence and through right attention, he attains such a concentration of mind that, with his mind thus concentrated,
he recollects his former lives, but does not recollect beyond that.
He speaks thus:
‘Those venerable devas who are not corrupted by play do not dwell excessively devoted to the nature of laughter, play, and delight.
As they do not dwell excessively devoted to the nature of laughter, play, and delight, their mindfulness does not fail.
Because their mindfulness does not fail, those devas do not fall away from that body.’
“They are permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain exactly so for all eternity.
But as for us, who were once corrupted by play— dwelling excessively devoted to the nature of laughter,
play, and delight— our mindfulness became lost while we dwelt thus, excessively devoted to laughter, play, and delight.”
‘Through a lapse of mindfulness, we have passed away from that body and,
being impermanent, unstable, short-lived, and subject to falling away, have come to this state. This, monks,

is the second ground on account of which, relying upon it and depending upon it, some recluses and brahmins who are partial-eternalists and partial-non-eternalists proclaim the self and the world to be partly eternal and partly non-eternal.

And on what basis, on what account, do those venerable recluses and brahmins, being some-of-eternalists and some-of-non-eternalists, proclaim the self and the world to be partly eternal and partly non-eternal?
There are, monks, certain gods called "Mind-Defiled" (*manopadosika*). They gaze excessively upon one another.
Gazing excessively upon one another, they become corrupt in mind toward one another. They [gaze] at one another...
With corrupted minds, their bodies exhausted and their minds exhausted, those devas fall from that host.
Now, monks, it is possible that a certain being, having fallen from that host, comes to this state of existence.
Having come to this state of existence, he goes forth from the home life into homelessness.
Having gone forth from the household life into homelessness, through ardor, exertion, application,
heedfulness, and right attention, he attains such a concentration of mind that,
with his mind thus concentrated, he recollects his former lives, but does not recollect beyond that.
Thus he spoke:
“Those venerable devas who are not corrupted by ill will do not gaze excessively upon one another.
Not gazing excessively upon one another, they do not corrupt their minds toward one another. They [behave] toward one another...”
With minds free from malice, their bodies untiring and their minds untiring, those devas do not fall away from that body;
they are permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change, remaining exactly as they are for all eternity.
But we, who were corrupted in mind, gazed excessively upon one another. Those...
‘By excessively gazing at one another, we corrupted our minds toward each other.
With our minds thus corrupted toward one another, we became weary in body and weary in mind.
Thus, having passed away from that body—being impermanent, unstable, short-lived, and subject to falling away—we have come to this state of existence.’”
This, monks, is the third ground, relying upon which and referring to which some recluses and brahmins proclaim the self and the world to be partly eternal and partly non-eternal.
And what, good sirs, is the fourth ground, relying upon which and referring to which some recluses and brahmins proclaim the self and the world to be partly eternal and partly non-eternal?
In this case, monks, a certain ascetic or brahmin is a rationalist and an investigator. Relying on his own reasoning and following the course of inquiry, he declares from his own intuition:
"That which is called 'the eye,' or 'the ear,' or 'the nose,' or 'the tongue,' or 'the body'—this self is impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, and subject to change."
"But as for this which is called 'mind' or 'mentality' or 'consciousness'—this self is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain exactly the same for all eternity.
This, monks, is the fourth position, based upon which and referring to which some recluses and brahmins proclaim the self and the world to be partly eternal and partly non-eternal.

“Monks, it is on these four grounds that those recluses and brahmins who are partial-eternalists and partial-non-eternalists proclaim the self and the world to be partly eternal and partly non-eternal.

For whatever recluses or brahmins, monks, there are who are partial-eternalists and partial-non-eternalists and proclaim the self and the world to be partly eternal and partly non-eternal, they all do so on these very same four grounds.”
[These views arise] from various grounds, or from one or another of these; there is nothing outside of this.
This, monks, the Tathāgata understands:
"These standpoints for views, thus grasped and thus adhered to, lead to such-and-such destinations and result in such-and-such future states."
The Tathāgata understands that, and he understands what is even more sublime than that; and understanding it, he does not cling to it. Because he does not cling, he has personally realized Nibbāna.
Having understood, as they truly are, the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding feelings, the Tathāgata, monks, is liberated through non-clinging.
These, monks, are those phenomena that are deep, hard to see, difficult to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of mere reasoning...
These are subtle points, to be understood by the wise, which the Tathāgata, having realized them for himself through direct knowledge, proclaims;
and it is concerning these that those who speak rightly would speak the true praise of the Tathāgata. 3.1.3.
The Doctrine of the Finite and Infinite.
“Bhikkhus, there are some recluses and brahmins who, as extensionists, proclaim the world to be finite or infinite on four grounds.
On what basis, with reference to what, do those worthy recluses and brahmins proclaim the world to be finite or infinite on four grounds?
Here, bhikkhus, a certain recluse or brahmin, through ardor, through exertion, through application... [continues]”
Through diligence and through right attention, he attains such a concentration of mind that, with his mind thus concentrated,
he dwells perceiving the world as finite.
He speaks thus:
‘This world is finite and circumscribed.

Why is that? Because by means of ardor, exertion, application, heedfulness, and right attention, I attain such a concentration of mind that, with my mind thus concentrated, I dwell perceiving the world as finite.’
"By this means I know this:
'This world is finite and circumscribed.

This, monks, is the first point by resorting to which, and depending on which, some recluses and brahmins who speculate about the finitude and infinity of the world proclaim the world to be finite and infinite.

And as for the second case, venerable sirs, on what basis and with reference to what do those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of finitude and infinity declare the world to be finite and infinite?
Here, monks, a certain ascetic or brahmin, through ardor, through exertion, through application, through diligence, and through right attention,
attains such a concentration of mind that, when his mind is thus concentrated...
Perceiving the mind as infinite, he dwells in the world.
He says this:
"This world is infinite and boundless."
Those ascetics and brahmins who say,
"This world is finite and circumscribed," speak falsely;
this world is infinite and boundless.
For what reason?

Because, through ardor, through striving, through application, through diligence, and through right attention, I attain such a concentration of mind that, with my mind thus concentrated, I dwell perceiving the world as infinite.
It is by this means that I know this.
‘Just as this world is infinite and boundless.

This, monks, is the second case on account of which, relying upon which, some ascetics and brahmins who hold views concerning the finite and infinite proclaim the world to be both finite and infinite.

And what, venerable sirs, do those ascetics and brahmins rely upon, what do they take as their basis, when they, holding views concerning the finite and infinite, proclaim the world to be both finite and infinite?
In this case, monks, a certain ascetic or brahmin, through ardor, through striving, through application, through diligence, and through right attention,
attains such a concentration of mind that, with his mind thus concentrated,
he dwells perceiving the world as finite above and below, and as infinite across.
Thus he spoke:
"This world is both finite and infinite.
As for those ascetics and brahmins who speak thus:"
“The world is finite and circumscribed,” they say— this is false.
And those ascetics and brahmins who say,
“The world is infinite and boundless,” their words too are false.
"This world is both finite and infinite.
For what reason?
Because, through ardor, through striving, through application, through heedfulness, and through right attention..."
I attain such a concentration of mind that, with my mind thus concentrated, I dwell perceiving the world as finite above and below,
and infinite across.
By this means I know this:
‘In this way the world is both finite and infinite.
This, monks, is the third case; depending on this, referring to this, some recluses and brahmins who are speculators about the finite and infinite proclaim the world to be both finite and infinite.

And as for the fourth case, venerable sirs, depending on what, referring to what, do those recluses and brahmins who are speculators about the finite and infinite proclaim the world to be both finite and infinite?

In this case, monks, a certain ascetic or brahmin is a reasoner and an investigator. Relying on his own reasoning and following the course of his investigation, he speaks according to his own inspiration:
"This world is neither finite nor infinite.
As for those ascetics and brahmins who say:..."
‘This world is finite and circumscribed,’ that is false.
And those recluses and brahmins who say,
‘This world is infinite and limitless,’ their claim too is false.
As for those ascetics and brahmins who say,
"This world is both finite and infinite," their words too are false.
This world is neither finite nor infinite.
“Monks, this is the fourth ground on account of which, relying upon which, some recluses and brahmins who are speculators about the finite and infinite proclaim the world to be finite and infinite.
It is on these four grounds, monks, that those recluses and brahmins who are speculators about the finite and infinite proclaim the world to be finite and infinite.

Whatever recluses or brahmins, monks, are speculators about the finite and infinite and proclaim the world to be finite and infinite, all of them do so on these very four grounds or on one of them; there is none outside of these.”
In this regard, monks, the Tathāgata understands:
“These standpoints for views, thus grasped and thus adhered to, lead to such a destination and such a future state.
The Tathāgata understands that, and he understands even more than that; yet he does not adhere to that understanding. And because he does not adhere to it, he has personally realized Nibbāna.
"Monks, having known as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding feelings, the Tathāgata is liberated through non-clinging.
Monks, these are those phenomena that are deep, hard to see, difficult to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of reasoning, subtle, and to be experienced by the wise;
which the Tathāgata, having realized them for himself through direct knowledge, makes known, and by which the Tathāgata..."
Those who speak correctly would speak of them as they truly are.

3.1.4. Evasive Sophistry: There are, monks, some recluses and brahmins who are evasive sophists; when questioned on various points, they resort to verbal equivocation and evasive sophistry based on four grounds.

And on what basis, monks, do those venerable recluses and brahmins, being questioned here and there, resort to verbal wrangling and the evasion of the deathless when asked a question on various points, by means of these four grounds?
Here, monks, a certain recluse or brahmin does not understand as it really is: “This is wholesome,” nor does he understand as it really is: “This is unwholesome.
It occurs to him:
‘Indeed, I do not understand as it really is: “This is wholesome,” nor do I understand as it really is:

“This is unwholesome. If, while not understanding as it really is that “this is wholesome” and not understanding as it really is that “this is unwholesome,” I were to declare, “This is wholesome,” or were to declare, “This is unwholesome,” that would be a falsehood for me.’
‘What would be a lie for me would be a vexation for me;
what is a vexation for me is an obstacle for me.

Thus, out of fear of lying and out of loathing for lying, he does not declare, ‘This is wholesome,’ nor does he declare, ‘This is unwholesome. When questioned on various points, he resorts to verbal evasion and to the endless equivocation of the Eel-Wriggler:
‘It is thus for me,’ I do not say; ‘it is so for me,’ I do not say; ‘it is otherwise for me,’ I do not say;

‘it is not for me,’ I do not say; ‘it is not not for me,’ I do not say. This, monks, is the first ground by resorting to which, by relying upon which, some recluses and brahmins who are endless equivocators, when questioned on this or that point, fall into verbal wrangling and endless equivocation.

And what, venerable sirs, is the second ground by resorting to which, by relying upon which, those recluses and brahmins who are endless equivocators, when questioned on this or that point, fall into verbal wrangling and endless equivocation?
“Here, monks, a certain ascetic or brahmin does not understand as it really is: ‘This is wholesome,’ nor does he understand as it really is:
‘This is unwholesome. It occurs to him:
‘I indeed do not understand as it really is: “This is wholesome,” nor do I understand as it really is: “This is unwholesome.”’”

If, moreover, while not understanding as it really is that "this is wholesome" and not understanding as it really is that "this is unwholesome," I were to declare "this is wholesome" or declare "this is unwholesome," then in that case there would be in me desire or lust, or hatred or aversion.
‘Wherever there might be in me desire or lust, or hatred or aversion, that would be my clinging.
What is my clinging, that would be my affliction.
What is my affliction, that would be my obstacle.’”

Thus, out of fear of clinging and out of loathing for clinging, he does not declare, "This is wholesome," nor does he declare, "This is unwholesome. When questioned on various points, he resorts to verbal evasion and to the "eel-wriggling" of the Eel-Wrigglers, saying:
"It is so for me, too; it is not so for me, either; it is otherwise for me, too; it is not otherwise for me, either; it is not for me, neither; it is not not for me, neither."

This, monks, is the second ground on account of which, relying upon which, some recluses and brahmins who are endless equivocators, when questioned here and there, resort to verbal equivocation and to endless equivocation.

And what, venerable sirs, do those recluses and brahmins rely upon, what do they take as their basis, whereby—being endless equivocators—they, when questioned here and there, resort to verbal equivocation and to endless equivocation?
In this case, monks, a certain ascetic or brahmin does not understand as it really is: "This is wholesome," nor does he understand as it really is: "This is unwholesome.
It occurs to him:
"I do not understand as it really is that 'this is wholesome,' nor do I understand as it really is that 'this is unwholesome.'"
If, while not understanding as it really is that "this is wholesome" and not understanding as it really is that "this is unwholesome," I were nevertheless to declare,

"this is wholesome," or to declare, "this is unwholesome"— for there are indeed ascetics and brahmins who are wise, subtle, skilled in the doctrines of others, and like hair-splitters; they move about as if piercing through views with the sword of wisdom,
and they would cross-examine, interrogate, and rebuke me on that point.
‘If they were to question me there, examine me, and cross-examine me, I might not be able to answer them.
That I am unable to answer them would be a source of distress for me;
that distress would be an obstacle for me.’”

Thus, out of fear of being cross-examined and out of loathing for being cross-examined, he neither declares, "This is wholesome," nor does he declare, "This is unwholesome. When questioned on various points, he resorts to verbal evasion and to the "eel-wriggling" of the Eel-Wrigglers:
"It is so for me, too; it is not so for me, either; it is otherwise for me, too; it is not thus for me, either; it is not not so for me, either."

This, monks, is the third ground on account of which, relying upon it, some recluses and brahmins who are proponents of endless equivocation, when questioned here and there, resort to verbal wrangling and to endless equivocation.

And what, venerable sirs, is the fourth ground on account of which those recluses and brahmins who are proponents of endless equivocation, when questioned here and there, resort to verbal wrangling and to endless equivocation?
Here, monks, a certain recluse or brahmin is dull-witted and confused.
Thus, due to dullness and delusion, when questioned on various points, he resorts to verbal evasion and theeel-wriggling of an eel:
"If you ask me, 'Is there another world?'—if I thought 'there is another world,' I would declare to you, 'There is another world. But I do not say so;
nor do I say it is otherwise; nor do I say it is not so; nor do I say it is not not so."
‘There is no other world... ... ‘Both there is and there is not another world... ...
‘Neither is there nor is there not another world... ... [and so forth].
‘There are beings who are spontaneously reborn’ … ‘there are no beings who are spontaneously reborn’ … ‘there both are and are not beings who are spontaneously reborn’ … [and so forth].
‘There neither are nor are not beings who arise spontaneously’ … ‘There is fruit and result of good and evil deeds’ … ‘There is no fruit and result of good and evil deeds’ … [and so forth].
‘There both is and is not a fruit and result of good and bad deeds …pe… ‘There neither is nor is not a fruit and result of good and bad deeds …pe… ‘A Tathāgata exists after death …pe…’
‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death’ …pe… ‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death’ …pe… ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’—
if you ask me this, [I say: ‘Neither exists nor does not exist.’”
‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death’—if this were my view, then I would explain it to you as: ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.
But [since that is not so], I do not say “it is thus,” nor do I say “it is otherwise,” nor do I say “it is not so,” nor do I say “it is not not so.”

This, monks, is the fourth ground on account of which, relying upon it, some recluses and brahmins who are endless equivocators, when questioned here and there, resort to verbal equivocation and to endless equivocation.
It is by means of these four bases, monks, that those recluses and brahmins who are endless equivocators, when questioned here and there, resort to verbal equivocation and to endless equivocation.
Whatever recluses or brahmins, monks, are endless equivocators... [when questioned here and there]...
When questioned, they resort to verbal evasion and the "eel-wriggling" of the Amarāvakas;
all of them do so either by means of these four grounds or one of them, and there is nothing outside of this...
Those who would speak rightly of the Tathāgata’s true praise would speak thus.
3.1.5. The Doctrine of Fortuitous Origination:
“Bhikkhus, there are some recluses and brahmins who are fortuitous originists; on two grounds they proclaim that the self and the world have arisen by chance.”

And on what basis, with reference to what, do those worthy recluses and brahmins, being proponents of fortuitous origination, declare both the self and the world to have arisen fortuitously through two grounds?
There are, monks, certain deities called the non-percipient beings (*asaññasattā*).
Upon the arising of perception, those deities pass away from that realm.
"It is possible, monks, that some being, having passed away from that body, comes to this state of existence.
Having come to this state of existence, he goes forth from the home life into homelessness.
Having gone forth from the home life into homelessness, through ardor, through exertion, and through application..."
Through diligence and through right attention, he attains such a concentration of mind that, with his mind thus concentrated,
he recollects the arising of perception but does not recollect anything beyond that.
He says this:
‘The self and the world have arisen fortuitously.
For what reason?
Because previously I did not exist, and now, having not existed, I have undergone transformation into a state of being.’”
This, monks, is the first ground on account of which, relying upon which, some ascetics and brahmins who advocate fortuitous origination proclaim that the self and the world have arisen by chance.

And what, venerable sirs, do those other ascetics and brahmins rely upon, what do they take as their basis, when they advocate fortuitous origination and proclaim that the self and the world have arisen by chance?
Here, monks, a certain ascetic or brahmin is a rationalist, an investigator.
Thus, struck by reasoning and following from inquiry, he speaks from his own intuition:
"The self and the world have arisen fortuitously.

This, monks, is the second case, depending on which and referring to which, some recluses and brahmins who are proponents of fortuitous origination declare the self and the world to have arisen fortuitously.
“Monks, it is by means of these two grounds that those recluses and brahmins who are proponents of fortuitous origination declare the self and the world to be fortuitously originated.
For whatever recluses or brahmins, monks, are proponents of fortuitous origination and declare the self and the world to be fortuitously originated,
they all do so either by means of these very two grounds or by one or another of them.”
There is none outside of this [teaching]...
such that those who would speak rightly of the Tathāgata’s praise according to reality could do so.

“Monks, it is on these eighteen grounds that those recluses and brahmins who are speculators about the past, who hold views regarding the past, assert various doctrinal propositions concerning the past.
Whatever recluses or brahmins, monks, are speculators about the past, who hold views regarding the past,
and assert various doctrinal propositions concerning the past, they all do so on these very eighteen grounds.”
Or by one of these; there is nothing outside of this.
This, monks, the Tathāgata understands:
"These standpoints for views, thus grasped and thus adhered to, lead to such-and-such a destination and result in such-and-such a future state."
The Tathāgata understands that, and he understands even more than that; and understanding it, he does not cling to it. Through his non-clinging, he has personally realized Nibbāna.
Having understood, as they truly are, the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding feelings, the Tathāgata, monks, is liberated through non-clinging.
These, monks, are those phenomena that are deep, hard to see, difficult to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of mere reasoning...
These are subtle, to be experienced by the wise, which the Tathāgata, having realized them for himself through direct knowledge, proclaims;
and it is regarding these that those who speak rightly would speak the true praise of the Tathāgata.
This concludes the second recitation section.
3.2. Speculators Concerning the Future:

There are, monks, some recluses and brahmins who are speculators concerning the future, who hold views about the future, and who, based on the future, assert various kinds of speculative propositions on forty-four grounds.

On what basis, with reference to what, do those venerable recluses and brahmins, being speculators concerning the future, holding views about the future, assert various kinds of speculative propositions on forty-four grounds?

3.2.1. The Doctrine of Consciousness after Death: "Bhikkhus, there are some recluses and brahmins who maintain the doctrine of consciousness after death; on sixteen grounds, they describe the self as conscious after death.

And on what basis, with reference to what, do those venerable recluses and brahmins maintain the doctrine of consciousness after death, describing the self as conscious after death on sixteen grounds?"
‘The self is material and healthy after death, possessing perception,’ they declare.
‘The self is immaterial and healthy after death, possessing perception,’ they declare.
‘The self is both material and immaterial …’ [and so on].
‘The self is neither material nor immaterial … the self is finite … the self is infinite …’
‘The self is both finite and infinite…’ ‘The self is neither finite nor infinite…’ ‘The self possesses a singular perception…’
‘The self possesses diverse perceptions…’ ‘The self possesses limited perceptions…’ ‘The self possesses immeasurable perceptions…’
‘The self is exclusively happy…’ … ‘The self is exclusively suffering…’ … ‘The self is both happy and suffering…’
‘After death, the self is neither painful nor pleasant and is conscious,’ they declare.
It is on these sixteen grounds, monks, that those ascetics and brahmins who maintain a doctrine of consciousness after death proclaim the self to be conscious after death.
Whatever ascetics or brahmins, monks, there may be who maintain a doctrine of consciousness after death... [regarding] the state after death...
All those who describe a self as possessing perception do so on one or another of these sixteen grounds;
there is nothing outside of these. … [as before] …
Those who would speak of the Tathāgata in accordance with reality, speaking rightly, would speak thus. 3.2.2.
The Doctrine of Non-perception.
There are, monks, some recluses and brahmins who maintain a doctrine of non-perception after death; they describe the self as non-perceiving after death on eight grounds.

And on what basis, with reference to what, do those venerable recluses and brahmins, based on eight grounds, proclaim a doctrine of non-percipient existence after death, describing the self as non-percipient after death?
They describe it thus: "The self is possessed of form, healthy, and non-percipient after death.
They describe it thus: "The self is formless, healthy, and non-percipient after death."
‘The self is both material and immaterial …pe….
‘The self is neither material nor immaterial ….
‘The self is finite ….’
‘The self is infinite…’ ‘The self is both finite and infinite…’ ‘The self is neither finite nor infinite,
healthy after death, and non-percipient,’ they declare.
“Monks, it is on these eight grounds that those ascetics and brahmins who maintain the doctrine of non-perception after death proclaim the self to be non-percipient after death.
Whatever ascetics or brahmins, monks, maintain the doctrine of non-perception after death and proclaim the self to be non-percipient after death,
they all do so on these very eight grounds or on one or another of them.”
There is none outside of this [teaching]...
such that those who would speak rightly of the Tathāgata’s true praise could do so.

3.2.3. The Doctrine of Neither-Conscious-Nor-Unconscious “There are, bhikkhus, some recluses and brahmins who are speculators about the state beyond death as neither-conscious-nor-unconscious; they describe the self as neither-conscious-nor-unconscious after death on eight grounds.

On what basis, with reference to what, do those worthy recluses and brahmins, being speculators about the state beyond death as neither-conscious-nor-unconscious, describe the self as neither-conscious-nor-unconscious after death on eight grounds?”
‘The self is material, healthy after death, and neither percipient nor non-percipient,’ they declare.
‘The self is immaterial …’ ‘The self is both material and immaterial …’
‘The self is neither material nor immaterial ….
‘The self is finite ….
‘The self is infinite ….’
‘The self is both finite and infinite…’ ‘After death,
the self is neither finite nor infinite, healthy, and neither percipient nor non-percipient’— thus they declare.

It is on these eight grounds, monks, that those recluses and brahmins who maintain doctrines concerning the state beyond death as neither percipient nor non-percipient declare the self to be neither percipient nor non-percipient after death.

"Whatever recluses or brahmins, bhikkhus, who maintain the doctrine of neither-perception-nor-non-perception after death, and who describe the self as neither-perceiving-nor-non-perceiving after death, all of them do so on these eight grounds...
[as before] ...which those speaking rightly would speak as the true praise of the Tathāgata."
3.2.4. Annihilationism “Bhikkhus, there are some recluses and brahmins who are annihilationists; they proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being on seven grounds.

On what basis, with reference to what, do those venerable recluses and brahmins, as annihilationists, proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being on these seven grounds?”
In this case, monks, some ascetic or brahmin holds such a doctrine and such a view:

“Sirs, when this self—which possesses form, is composed of the four great elements, and is born of mother and father—is cut off and destroyed at the breaking up of the body, and does not exist after death; to this extent, sirs, this self is completely annihilated.
In this way, some proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.
Then another said this:
“Sir, there indeed is that self of which you speak; I do not say that it does not exist.
However, sir, this self is not completely annihilated by that much alone.”
"There is, sir, another self that is divine, material, belonging to the sense sphere, and subsisting on physical food.
You do not know it and you do not see it;
I know it and I see it."
"Thus, sir, when at the breaking up of the body this self is cut off, perishes, and does not exist after death—to this extent, sir, this self is completely annihilated.
In this way, some proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.
To them, another says this:
“Sir, there is indeed this self that you speak of; I do not say that it does not exist.
However, sir, this self is not completely annihilated by that much alone.
For there is, sir, another self—divine, material, mind-made, complete in all its limbs and parts, with all faculties unimpaired.”
‘You do not know that, you do not see that; I know it, I see it.
That self, sir, when at the breaking up of the body is cut off, perishes, and does not exist after death—to this extent, sir, this self is completely annihilated.’”
In this regard, some proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.
Another says to him:
“Sir, there indeed is that self of which you speak; I do not say that it does not exist.”
But, sir, this self is not completely annihilated by that much.

There is, sir, another self which, with the complete transcendence of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory resistance, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking "space is infinite," reaches the sphere of infinite space.
You do not know it, you do not see it.
‘I know that self; I see it.
That self, sir, is annihilated and destroyed with the breakup of the body, and does not exist after death. To this extent, sir, this self is completely annihilated.
In this way, some proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.
Another said this to him:
“Sir, there is indeed this self of which you speak; I do not say that it does not exist.
However, sir, this self is not completely annihilated by that much.”
"There is, sir, another self that, having completely transcended the base of infinite space, enters upon and abides in the base of infinite consciousness, [perceiving] 'consciousness is infinite.
You do not know it, you do not see it;
I know it, I see it."
"Thus, sir, when this self is cut off and perishes at the breaking up of the body and does not exist after death, to that extent, sir, this self is completely annihilated.
In this way, some describe the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.
To them, another says this:
“Sir, there indeed is that self of which you speak; I do not say that it does not exist.
Yet, sir, this self is not completely annihilated by that much alone.
There is, sir, another self that, having entirely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, reaches the base of nothingness, thinking, ‘There is nothing.’”
‘You do not know that, you do not see that; I know it, I see it.
That self, sir, when at the breaking up of the body is cut off, perishes, and does not exist after death—to this extent, sir, this self is completely annihilated.’”
In this way, some proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.
Another says to him:
“Sir, there indeed is that self of which you speak; I do not say that it does not exist.”
But, sir, this self is not completely annihilated by that much.

There is, sir, another self which, having completely transcended the base of nothingness, thinking "this is peaceful, this is sublime," enters upon and abides in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
You do not know it, you do not see it.
‘I know that self; I see it.
That self, friends, is annihilated and destroyed with the breakup of the body and does not exist after death; to this extent, friends, this self is completely annihilated.
In this way, some proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.
"It is on these seven grounds, monks, that those recluses and brahmins who are annihilationists proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.

For whatever recluses or brahmins, monks, are annihilationists who proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being, they all do so on these very seven grounds... [as above] ...
Those who would speak rightly of the Tathāgata’s true qualities would speak thus. 3.2.5.
The Doctrine of Nibbāna in the Present Life:

“Bhikkhus, there are some recluses and brahmins who proclaim a doctrine of Nibbāna in the present life, and they describe the supreme Nibbāna in the present life for an existing being on five grounds.”

And on what basis, with reference to what, do those venerable recluses and brahmins, proponents of Nibbāna in the present life, proclaim the supreme Nibbāna in the present life for an existing being on five grounds?
Here, bhikkhus, a certain recluse or brahmin holds such a doctrine and such a view as this:
“When, sir, this self is endowed with and possessed of the five cords of sensual pleasure and enjoys them, to that extent, sir, this self has attained the supreme Nibbāna in the present life.”
In this way, some proclaim the supreme Nibbāna in this very life for an existing being.
Another says to him:
“Sir, there is indeed that self of which you speak; I do not say that it does not exist.”
But, sir, this self does not yet attain supreme Nibbāna in this very life. Why is that?
Because sensual pleasures, sir, are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change; with their change and alteration, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise.
‘But when, sir, this self, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states,
enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion— at that point, sir,
this self has attained the supreme Nibbāna in this very life.’”
In this regard, some proclaim the supreme Nibbāna in this very life for an existing being.
Another says to him:
"Sir, there is indeed this self of which you speak; I do not say that it does not exist."
But, sir, this self does not yet attain supreme Nibbāna in the present life to that extent.
And why is that? Because whatever is thought and deliberated upon therein is declared to be gross.
‘But when, sir, this self, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought,
enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which is internal serenity and unification of mind, free from applied and sustained thought, born of concentration,
and filled with rapture and happiness— at that point, sir, this self has attained the supreme Nibbāna in this very life.’”
In this way, some proclaim the supreme Nibbāna in this very life for an existing being.
Another says to him:
"Sir, there is indeed this self of which you speak; I do not say that it does not exist."
But, sir, this self does not yet attain supreme Nibbāna in this very life to that extent.
And why is that? Because whatever state of rapture there is, and whatever elation of mind, by that it is declared to be coarse.
"But when, sir, through the fading away of rapture, this self dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending,
and experiences happiness with the body— of which the Noble Ones declare, 'He who is equanimous and mindful dwells in happiness'—
and thus enters and abides in the third jhāna, to that extent, sir, this self has attained supreme Nibbāna in the present life."
In this way, some proclaim the supreme Nibbāna in the present life for an existing being.
Another says to him:
"Sir, there is indeed that self of which you speak; I do not say that it does not exist."
But, sir, this self has not yet attained supreme Nibbāna in this very life to that extent.
Why is that? Because the mental preoccupation with "this is happiness" therein makes it coarse.
‘But when, sir, this self— through the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief—
enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity,
it is to this extent, sir, that this self has attained the supreme Nibbāna in the present life.’”
“In this way, some proclaim the supreme Nibbāna in this very life for an existing being.
It is on these five grounds, monks, that those ascetics and brahmins who maintain the doctrine of Nibbāna in this very life proclaim the supreme Nibbāna in this very life for an existing being.

Whatever ascetics or brahmins, monks, maintain the doctrine of Nibbāna in this very life and proclaim the supreme Nibbāna in this very life for an existing being, they all do so on these same five grounds.”
those who would speak rightly of the Tathāgata’s true praise would speak thus.
