It is on these forty-four grounds, monks, that those recluses and brahmins who speculate about the future, hold views regarding the future, and assert various kinds of propositions concerning the future, do so.
"Whatever recluses or brahmins, bhikkhus, who speculate about the future, hold views regarding the future,
and assert various kinds of propositions concerning the future— all of them do so on account of these very forty-four bases..."
Those who would speak in accordance with reality when praising the Tathāgata would speak thus.
These, monks, are those recluses and brahmins who are speculators about the past, speculators about the future, speculators about both the past and the future,
who hold views regarding the past and the future, and who put forward various doctrinal propositions concerning the past and the future.
They declare [their views] by means of sixty-two bases.
For whatever ascetics or brahmins, bhikkhus, are speculators about the past, or speculators about the future,
or speculators about both the past and the future, who hold views regarding the past and the future, and who, concerning the past and the future, have formulated various kinds of [theories]:
They proclaim various positions of conviction; all of them do so by means of these very sixty-two bases, or one or another of them;
there is nothing outside of this.
This, monks, the Tathāgata understands.
‘These standpoints for views, thus grasped and thus adhered to, lead to such-and-such a destination and such-and-such a future state.
The Tathāgata understands this, and he understands even more than that; yet he does not misapprehend that understanding. Because he does not misapprehend it, he has personally realized Nibbāna.
Having understood, as they truly are, the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding feelings, the Tathāgata, monks, is liberated through non-clinging.
“Monks, these phenomena are indeed profound, difficult to see, difficult to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of mere reasoning,
subtle, and to be experienced by the wise; they are those which the Tathāgata, having realized them for himself through direct higher knowledge, proclaims,
and it is regarding these that those who would speak rightly of the Tathāgata’s true praise would speak.”
4. The Exposition on the Description of Self and World. 4.1. The Section on Agitation and Wavering.
In this regard, monks, those recluses and brahmins who are eternalists proclaim the self and the world to be eternal.
Based on these four grounds, that which is felt by those venerable recluses and brahmins— who do not know and do not see—
is merely the agitation and vacillation of those immersed in craving.
In this regard, bhikkhus, as for those recluses and brahmins who are partial-eternalists and partial-non-eternalists [asserting] that some things are eternal...
In one way or another, they proclaim the self and the world to be partly eternal and partly non-eternal on four grounds;
yet even that is merely the feeling, the agitation, and the vacillation of those venerable recluses and brahmins who do not know and do not see, being immersed in craving.
In this regard, monks, as for those recluses and brahmins who are speculators about the finite and infinite and who proclaim the world to be finite and infinite:
On these four grounds, that which is felt by those venerable recluses and brahmins— who do not know and do not see, who are immersed in craving—
is merely a state of agitation and vacillation. In this regard, monks,
those recluses and brahmins who are eel-wrigglers, when questioned on various points, [remain evasive].
They fall into the same kind of vacillation and the "eel-wriggling" regarding four points;
that too is merely the feeling of those venerable recluses and brahmins who do not know and do not see, being immersed in craving and characterized by agitation and wavering.
In this regard, monks, those recluses and brahmins who are proponents of fortuitous origination [assert] a self arisen by chance...

And they describe the world on two grounds; yet even that is merely the felt experience of those venerable recluses and brahmins who do not know and do not see, being immersed in craving and subject to agitation and vacillation.
In this regard, monks, those recluses and brahmins who are speculators about the past, who hold views regarding the past, [speculate] about the past...
Based on these, they assert various kinds of speculative views regarding eighteen grounds;
yet that is merely the feeling of those venerable recluses and brahmins who do not know and do not see, being immersed in craving and merely the agitation and vacillation of one who is terrified.
In this regard, bhikkhus, as for those recluses and brahmins who maintain the doctrine of percipient immortality after death...
They describe a self possessing perception in sixteen ways;
yet even that is merely the felt experience of those venerable recluses and brahmins who do not know and do not see, being caught in craving and agitated by it.
In this regard, bhikkhus, those recluses and brahmins who maintain a doctrine of non-perception after death [claim] that after death...
They describe the self as non-percipient on eight grounds;
yet even that is merely the feeling of those venerable recluses and brahmins who do not know and do not see, being immersed in craving and caught up in agitation and vacillation.
In this regard, bhikkhus, those recluses and brahmins who maintain the doctrine of neither-perception-nor-non-perception after death [regard] the state after death...
They describe the self as neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient on eight grounds;
yet even that is merely the feeling of those venerable recluses and brahmins who do not know and do not see, being immersed in craving and subject to agitation and vacillation.
In this regard, monks, those recluses and brahmins who are annihilationists [assert] the cutting off and destruction of an existing being...

They proclaim annihilation on seven grounds; yet that too is merely the feeling of those venerable recluses and brahmins who do not know and do not see, being immersed in craving and agitated by fear.
In this regard, bhikkhus, as for those recluses and brahmins who assert Nibbāna in the present life for an existing being, their supreme Nibbāna in the present life for an existing being—

They proclaim [this] on five grounds; yet even that is merely the felt experience of those venerable recluses and brahmins who do not know and do not see, being driven by craving and agitated by restlessness.
In this regard, bhikkhus, as for those recluses and brahmins who are speculators about the future, who hold views regarding the future... [speculating about] the future.
Based on these, they assert various kinds of speculative views concerning forty-four points;
yet that is merely the feeling of those venerable recluses and brahmins who do not know and do not see, being immersed in craving and characterized by agitation and vacillation.
In this regard, monks, as for those recluses and brahmins who are speculators about the past, speculators about the future, and speculators about both the past and the future—
And those who hold views concerning the past and the future, who assert various speculative propositions regarding the past and the future based on sixty-two grounds—
that too is merely the feeling of those venerable recluses and brahmins who do not know and do not see;
it is the agitation and vacillation of those immersed in craving.

4.2. The Section on Conditionality by Contact (Phassapaccayāvāra) In this regard, monks, those ascetics and brahmins who, on four grounds, proclaim the self and the world to be eternal—this too is conditioned by contact.
In this regard, monks, those ascetics and brahmins who, on four grounds, proclaim the self and the world to be partly eternal and partly non-eternal—this too is conditioned by contact.
In this regard, monks, those recluses and brahmins who, on four grounds, proclaim the world to be finite or infinite—this too is conditioned by contact.

In this regard, monks, those recluses and brahmins who are eel-wrigglers, when questioned on various points, resort to verbal evasion and eel-wriggling on four grounds—this too is conditioned by contact.

In this regard, monks, those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of fortuitous origination and who, on two grounds, describe the self and the world as originating by chance—that too is conditioned by contact.

In this regard, monks, those ascetics and brahmins who are speculators about the past, who hold views regarding the past, and who assert various doctrinal positions concerning the past on eighteen grounds—that too is conditioned by contact.

In this regard, monks, those recluses and brahmins who hold views concerning existence after death and who, on sixteen grounds, describe the self as conscious after death—that too is conditioned by contact.

In this regard, monks, those recluses and brahmins who hold views concerning existence after death and who, on eight grounds, describe the self as unconscious after death—that too is conditioned by contact.

In this regard, monks, those recluses and brahmins who maintain the doctrine of neither-perception-nor-non-perception after death, and who on eight grounds describe the self as neither-perceiving-nor-non-perceiving after death—that too is conditioned by contact.

In this regard, monks, those recluses and brahmins who are annihilationists, and who on seven grounds describe the destruction, annihilation, and non-existence of an existing being—that too is conditioned by contact.

In this regard, monks, those ascetics and brahmins who proclaim a Nibbāna in the present life for an existing being, and who describe that supreme Nibbāna in the present life on five grounds— that too is conditioned by contact. In this regard, monks,
those ascetics and brahmins who are speculators about the future, who hold views regarding the future,
and who assert various kinds of doctrinal positions concerning the future on forty-four grounds— that too is conditioned by contact.
In this regard, monks, those ascetics and brahmins who are speculators about the past,
speculators about the future, speculators about both the past and the future, and who hold views concerning the past and the future,
asserting various doctrinal positions based on sixty-two grounds— that too is conditioned by contact.

4.3. The Chapter on the Impossibility of This Position In this regard, monks, as for those ascetics and brahmins who are eternalists and who, on four grounds, proclaim the self and the world to be eternal—it is impossible that they could experience [that state] apart from contact.
In this regard, monks, as for those ascetics and brahmins who are partial-eternalists and partial-non-eternalists, [and who proclaim] one part to be eternal...
Some proclaim the self and the world to be partly eternal and partly non-eternal on four grounds;
that they will experience [this] apart from contact—such a case is impossible.

In this regard, monks, as for those recluses and brahmins who are speculators about the finite and infinite and who proclaim the finitude and infinity of the world on four grounds—that they will experience [this] apart from contact—such a case is impossible.
In this regard, monks, as for those recluses and brahmins who are endless equivocators, when questioned on various points,
they resort to verbal equivocation and the evasion of the issue through four grounds—
it is impossible that they could experience anything other than contact.
In this regard, monks, as for those recluses and brahmins who are proponents of fortuitous origination and who,
on two grounds, describe the self and the world as fortuitously originated— it is impossible that they will experience [anything] apart from contact.
In this regard, monks, as for those recluses and brahmins who are speculators about the past, who hold views concerning the past, and [who speculate about] the past...
Based on this, they assert various kinds of speculative views regarding the state after death through eighteen grounds.
It is impossible that they could experience [rebirth] apart from contact.
In this regard, monks, those ascetics and brahmins who maintain the doctrine of conscious post-mortem existence (uddhamāghātanika-saññīvāda) [assert that there is a self] after death...
They describe a self possessing perception in sixteen ways; that they would experience [it] apart from contact—this is impossible.
In this regard, bhikkhus, those recluses and brahmins who maintain the doctrine of non-perception after death, [regarding] what is beyond the grave...
They describe the self as non-percipient on eight grounds; that they would experience [anything] apart from contact—this is impossible.
In this regard, monks, those ascetics and brahmins who maintain the doctrine of neither-perception-nor-non-perception after death, regarding the state beyond death:
They describe the self as neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient on eight grounds; yet it is impossible that they could experience this apart from contact.
In this regard, monks, those recluses and brahmins who are annihilationists [assert] the cutting off and destruction of an existing being...
They proclaim non-existence on seven grounds; it is impossible that they could experience [anything] apart from contact.
In this regard, monks, those ascetics and brahmins who maintain the doctrine of Nibbāna in the present life claim the supreme Nibbāna for an existing being in the very present life.
They proclaim [their views] on five grounds; that they will experience [feeling] apart from contact—this is impossible.

In this regard, monks, those recluses and brahmins who are speculators about the future, who hold views regarding the future, and who assert various doctrinal propositions concerning the future on forty-four grounds—they, indeed...
"It is impossible that they will experience [feeling] apart from contact.
In this regard, monks, those ascetics and brahmins who are speculators about the past, speculators about the future, speculators about both the past and the future,
and who hold various views regarding the past and the future, have formulated numerous propositions concerning the past and the future.
They declare [their views] on sixty-two grounds; it is impossible that they could experience [the results] apart from contact.
4.4. Discourse on the Cycle Based on the Adherence to Views:

In this regard, monks, those recluses and brahmins who are eternalists and proclaim the self and the world to be eternal on four grounds, and those recluses and brahmins who are partial-eternalists and partial-non-eternalists... [and so forth].
Those ascetics and brahmins who hold views concerning the finite and infinite;
those ascetics and brahmins who are eel-wrigglers;
and those ascetics and brahmins who maintain the doctrine of fortuitous origination.
Those ascetics and brahmins who are speculators about the past...
those ascetics and brahmins who maintain the doctrine of conscious existence after death...
those ascetics and brahmins who maintain the doctrine of unconscious existence after death...
Those ascetics and brahmins who maintain the doctrine of neither-perception-nor-non-perception after death;
those ascetics and brahmins who maintain the doctrine of annihilationism;
and those ascetics and brahmins who maintain the doctrine of Nibbāna in this very life.
Those ascetics and brahmins who are speculators about the future...
those ascetics and brahmins who are speculators about the past, speculators about the future, speculators about both the past and the future,
who hold various views regarding the past and the future, and who put forward numerous speculative propositions concerning the past and the future.
They advocate on sixty-two grounds; all of them, having repeatedly contacted through the six bases of contact, experience feelings.
With feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth;
and with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be.
5. Discourse on Turning Away, etc.

Monks, when a monk understands, as they truly are, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the six bases of contact, he understands more excellently than all those [others].
For whatever ascetics or brahmins, monks, are speculators about the past or speculators about the future, [they are all surpassed by him].

Whether they are speculators about the past and the future, or hold views regarding the past and the future, and assert various kinds of propositions concerning the past and the future—all of them are caught within the net by these sixty-two grounds;
emerging, they emerge only from here; being included, they emerge only as those caught within the net.
“Just as if, monks, a skilled fisherman or a fisherman’s apprentice were to cover a small pool with a fine-meshed net, it would occur to him:
‘Whatever large creatures there are in this pool, they are all caught within the net.
They are trapped here; wherever they surface, they surface right here; wherever they are contained, they are contained right here.’”
“...as if emerging from within a net, they emerge. In the same way, monks,
whatever ascetics or brahmins are speculators about the past, or speculators about the future,
or speculators about both the past and the future, who hold views regarding the past and the future, and who, concerning the past and the future, [propound] various kinds of...
Whatever words of speculative views they may profess, all of them are encompassed within these sixty-two bases;
they emerge only from within this net, and being included therein and encompassed by this very net, they emerge as they emerge.
Monks, the body of the Tathāgata remains with the tether to existence severed.
"As long as his body remains, so long will gods and humans behold him.
But with the breakup of the body, after the exhaustion of life, gods and humans shall no longer behold him.
Just as, bhikkhus, when the stalk of a cluster of mangoes is cut, whatever mangoes were attached to that stalk all follow along with it."
"In the same way, monks, the body of the Tathāgata remains with the conduit to existence cut off;
as long as his body shall remain, so long will gods and humans behold it.
But with the breaking up of the body, after the exhaustion of life, gods and humans shall no longer behold it."
When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:
“It is wonderful, Bhante! It is marvelous, Bhante! What is the name of this discourse on the Dhamma?
“Therefore, Ānanda, you should remember this discourse on the Dhamma as ‘The Net of Meaning’ (Atthajāla), or as ‘The Net of the Dhamma’ (Dhammajāla).”
“Remember it as ‘The Brahmajāla’; remember it as ‘The Net of Views’; and remember it as ‘The Unsurpassed Victory in Battle.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Elated, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
And while this exposition was being spoken, the ten-thousandfold world system trembled.
The Brahmajāla Sutta is finished; it is the first.
